newsitem.title: USA: U.S. producers see lowest crude output in 42 years.
newsitem.headline: U.S. producers see lowest crude output in 42 years.

text.p: Independent producers expect U.S. crude oil production to hit 6.39 million barrels per day in 1997, the lowest domestic output in 42 years, the Independent Petroleum Association of America said on Friday.

Oil and products imports are expected to rise to 51.5 percent of domestic consumption next year to meet estimated petroleum demand of 18.4 million barrels per day, the trade group said in an annual supply-demand forecast.

"Inventories of all the petroleum products have declined to levels not seen since the early eighties," the association said. "While these situations are not critical, they have been followed much more closely because the supply cushion is nearly gone in the United States."

Domestic natural gas production is expected to grow to 19.1 trillion cubic feet, virtually unchanged from the past two years, and start-of-winter inventory levels are expected to be at the lowest levels in the past five years, the Washington, D.C.-based association said.

"While there has been a resurgence of gas-directed exploration and development in the offshore Gulf of Mexico, much of this natural gas won't become available until 1997 and 1998," the association said in its forecast, which is compiled by a committee of oil and gas producers.

Domestic energy consumption continues to surge, increasing 2.5 percent in 1996 to 89.49 quadrillion British thermal units, or quads, fueled by cold weather last winter. Consumption in 1997 is expected to rise 0.9 percent to 90.28 quads, the association said.

Although U.S. energy consumption growth will slow in 1997, real economic activity measured by inflation-adjusted Gross Domestic Product is expected to rise at an annual rate of 2.5 percent in 1996 and 2.1 percent in 1997.
"With few exceptions, the ratio of energy use per unit of GDP has been on a declining trend since the early 1970s," said the trade group, which has published its supply-demand forecasts since 1937.
